whatWorkedBest.pattern: Prediction giveaways tied to a huge real-world event
whatWorkedBest.evidence: The 3 World Cup Final prediction posts (5.4K–7.7K views) are the single best-performing content type found — all beat every other post by a wide margin.
whatWorkedBest.why: Two things stack: (1) a live, massive, real-world moment everyone's already talking about, and (2) a low-effort way to participate (comment a guess) with a real, specific prize.

whatWorkedBest.pattern: Large prize-pool giveaways, even without a cultural tie-in
whatWorkedBest.evidence: The $5,000,000 giveaway announcement (Nov 2025) hit 7,158 views on its own — the outright highest of all 12 posts, with no external event riding shotgun.
whatWorkedBest.why: Prize size alone can substitute for a cultural moment if it's big enough to feel newsworthy by itself.

whatWorkedLeast.evidence: The drawdown-types explainer (581 views) and the generic brand value-prop post (417 views) are the two lowest performers found — roughly 10–18x fewer views than the top giveaway posts.
whatWorkedLeast.why: No hook, no incentive to engage, no reason to comment or share — it's useful information but reads as a pamphlet, not a post.

whatWorkedLeast.pattern: Winner announcements buried in reply threads
whatWorkedLeast.evidence: The 'S2L Ultra Plan Winners' post (215 views) was published as a reply under the main winners post, not as its own standalone post — it's the single lowest view count found, even lower than plain educational content.
whatWorkedLeast.why: Replies get a fraction of the reach of a standalone post algorithmically, regardless of how good the content is.

recommendations: Lean further into prediction/giveaway formats tied to real, live cultural moments — not just trading news. GTA 6's Nov 19 launch is the next one of this scale (see Trend Radar).
Don't post educational content standalone. Wrap the same information (e.g. drawdown types) inside a giveaway, quiz, or 'guess which rule' format instead of a plain explainer.
Never post winner announcements as replies. Each one should be its own standalone post — it's real proof of payout, which is exactly the trust-building content that's hard to fake.
Test whether meme-style content works at all — there's currently zero data either way since the account hasn't tried it.
